doc.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015

chapter: Sinatra and the feel of time
title: Christina Aguilera and Frank Sinatra on honoring the song
summary: Finck criticizes over-embellishment, praises Sinatra's handling of words and tells the Cole Porter letter story.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Yeah. [sings distorted notes]. And it’s amazing. And I sat there and I said just sing the song. Can’t you just sing the song? Otherwise write your own. Because it didn’t make it more emotional, it didn’t deliver anything more, it was just her being about her. And you know I get upset by this stuff because if it’s a song I really like and somebody does that I’m like oh God, why are you doing that. Frank Sinatra, in my opinion, probably one of the greatest musicians I could think of, had a way of making the song present itself. I know he’s been accused of changing words or some of his renditions aren’t to my taste. But the bulk of his work is unsurpassed. And many times when he changed a word I think he had a good reason for doing that. Some words swing harder than others. If you say “the” it doesn’t swing. “That” has punctuation at the end and if you place that in the right place it makes a difference. Granted Cole Porter may not have written the word “that,” but I think Frank knew some stuff that a lot of people didn’t know. And actually there’s a very funny story because Cole Porter got upset with Frank changing some of the words and he sent Frank a letter saying if you can’t sing my songs as I wrote them, please don’t sing them.
